description: We are passionate about space, science and technology. We joined NASA Space Apps Challenge to learn new skills, explore real world scientific problems, and collaborate on creative solutions. Our goal is to develop an interactive platform that helps people understand microgravity combustion and fire safety through scientific data and AI.

details:
Flame Lab

Flame Lab, also called Flame in Freefall, is a web application by team AstronovaTech for the fire safety challenge of the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It brings NASA research on combustion in microgravity and partial gravity into one site where visitors can ask questions, read the original evidence and watch a model flame respond to different conditions. The application is available at https://flame-lab-pied.vercel.app.

Evidence base

Everything on the site rests on a curated database of 10 experiment records, 21 indexed documents and 92 indexed passages drawn from NASA reports, papers and web pages. Every fact carries a source ID, an exact location in the source and an evidence class, such as measured value, derived result, published interpretation, historical case or technology transfer. Values that a source does not state are marked as missing.

AI Research Analyst

The AI Research Analyst answers questions about fire and combustion in space. For each question, the server selects the most relevant passages from the database and searches three official NASA websites: nasa.gov, science.nasa.gov and ntrs.nasa.gov. The language model, Gemini 3.5 Flash, receives only that evidence and cannot browse the web. Every claim in an answer cites a passage, and each citation opens the quoted text with its source and location. Citations that do not match the evidence are rejected, and the answer is shown as plain text. When the evidence does not cover a question, the analyst says so.

The API keys are kept on the server. Ten key slots back each other up: if one key fails, the next answers, and if all of them fail, the site answers from the local database. Six example questions help new users start.

3-D Flame Simulator

The Simulator computes a round gas flame burning from an 8 mm nozzle, live in the browser. The model is a low-Mach, axisymmetric flow solver on a grid 36 mm wide and 110 mm tall with 1 mm cells, and it runs in a background thread so the page stays smooth. A ray-marched renderer turns the result into a 3-D flame that users can rotate by dragging or with the arrow keys, and the camera frames the flame automatically as it grows or shrinks.

Users can set gravity, oxygen level, pressure, ambient temperature, fuel flow and air flow, or choose a preset: Earth, Moon, Mars, microgravity or low oxygen. Four fuels are available, each with its own appearance. Hydrogen burns blue. Methane and ethanol are blue with a yellow-orange tip. Propane, the sootiest fuel, glows yellow-orange above a blue base and turns orange in microgravity. A readout under the flame gives its height, width, peak gas temperature and a model soot value.

A side-by-side view shows the same flame on Earth and in microgravity, with only gravity changed. At the default settings, the methane flame is about 7 mm tall and 8 mm wide on Earth, and about 13 mm tall and 16 mm wide in microgravity, where it is wider and rounder, as NASA experiments report. Ten experiment cards copy the gravity, pressure, oxygen and air flow of a documented NASA test into the model in one tap, and the flame then shows which experiment its conditions come from. A section titled “What each setting does” explains each control in plain language, and the current state can be exported as JSON.

Safety

The Safety page covers fourteen fire-safety themes. Examples include why Earth flammability tests can underestimate the risk in space, why slow ventilation airflow is the most dangerous, why turning off ventilation does not always put a fire out, why toxic gases may matter more than heat, and why lunar gravity may be the worst case. Each theme has a short summary, key figures with their passage IDs, open questions, the quoted NASA passages, and, where it exists, evidence that points the other way. Key figures include the lowest oxygen for upward burning of Mylar G (21.2% at 1 g, 15.6% at lunar gravity) and the gas speed with the highest flame spread (about 10 cm/s). A question bar at the top of the page and a button on each theme send questions to the AI Analyst.

Records and Compare

The Records section holds ten experiment records, X1 to X10. They cover the Saffire experiments, SoFIE, ACME, FM2, the Droplet Combustion Experiment and ground tests on PMMA at reduced pressure. Each record keeps the original wording, units and location in its source, marks every value as measured, derived, assumed or planned, and links to the sources and to the related safety themes. Records can be searched, filtered by gravity, explained with the AI, or opened in the Compare tool.

Compare places any two records side by side with charts. The comparison can be exported as a report to print or save as PDF, as an HTML file, or as CSV data.

About and limitations

The About section describes the methods and the evidence classes. It includes a reliability table and a list of limitations. The flame model is not validated, because the database contains no measured sizes of gas jet flames to compare it with. The flame colours are illustrative, not measured light emission. The real experiments burned solids and droplets, while the model always burns a gas, so it shows trends, not replays of the experiments.

Design and access

The interface uses glass panels over a live space background with stars, planets and galaxies, and the top bar keeps the same size on every page. On phones and tablets, the flame fills the screen and scrolls with the page, and its settings open in a bottom sheet. Asking a question takes the user straight to the answer. The site is available in English, Arabic (right to left) and Hindi, and it supports keyboard use and reduced motion.

Hosting

The site is hosted on Vercel, with the static page and one serverless function for the AI answers. The source code is in a private GitHub repository, and every update to the main branch is published to the live site automatically.
